newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers still at odds over EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers still at odds over EMU budget pact.

text.p: A drive to ensure sound economics once the European Union adopts a single currency is set to continue after EU finance ministers failed to settle remaining differences over an accord.
The ministers said on Monday they would reconvene on December 12 in Dublin, on the eve of a meeting of EU leaders, in the hope that a deal on budgetary discipline could be put on the table.
"There is a will and a desire to make considerable progress in Dublin...We want a proper agreement," Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn, current chairman of the EU finance ministers, said.

The main bone of contention is a definition of "exceptional and temporary" economic circumstances that would allow a country's budget deficit to exceed three percent of its gross domestic product (GDP).
Countries breaching the three percent threshold under a common currency could initially be fined 0.2 percent of GDP, with a maximum penalty set at 0.5 percent of total output.

Germany, supported by the Netherlands, has been insistent that there must be a strict, numerical definition of such circumstances, fearing that any other option could pave the way for political fudging which would weaken the pact.

Bonn has asked that the magnitude of such an extraordinary decline in growth be specified at two percent, but others among the 15-nation bloc have resisted the figure on the grounds that it is too rigid.
The Irish EU presidency suggested a compromise that avoids setting figures to the decline in output but requires that "significantly negative growth" be supported by strong statistical evidence.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect of the stability pact, said agreement next week on a budget pact would be desirable, but that he would not seek it at any cost.
He added that a definition of exceptional circumstances would have to be "calculable, clear and recognisable".

Germany's tough negotiating stance, which appeared to show signs of softening on Monday, has put it at odds with many of its EU partners, some of whom see the economic powerhouse too narrowly focused on the monetary aspects of a single currency.
Such differences in philosophy flared up last week in France when several senior monetary officials questioned the wisdom of linking Paris' economic and currency policies too closely to Germany's.

An agreement on a budget pact next week would also allow the EU to bring forward legislation on other important aspects of monetary union, including a new Exchange Rate Mechanism that links the single currency to those not participating at the start in 1999.
Officials said they had reached an agreement on the blueprint for a new ERM and had also secured a deal on the legal framework for a single currency.
